script.title: Why Braille Made Night Writing Simple

lines: A blind twelve-year-old runs his fingertip over an army code of dots.
His name is Louis Braille.
At three, he stabbed his eye with an awl in his father's harness shop.
By five, he was blind in both eyes.
At school in Paris, books have huge raised letters.
Students trace them slowly. They cannot write.
Then retired army captain Charles Barbier brings his night writing.
It was a code for soldiers to read in the dark.
Twelve raised dots stand for sounds.
But soldiers found it too hard.
You see, it's like knowing a friend's face at a glance, not inch by inch.
Barbier's code is too tall to read with one fingertip.
So Louis spends two years improving it.
He cuts it to six dots, three high and two wide.
Each pattern now stands for a letter, not a sound.
It fits under one fingertip, so a reader feels a whole letter at once.
With Barbier's own slate and stylus, students can finally write.
But the teachers refuse his code.
Louis dies at 43.
Two years later, his students finally get the school to adopt it.
A sharp point took his sight. Six tiny points gave millions a way to read.

claims.claim: At age three Louis Braille stabbed his eye with an awl in his father's harness shop and was blind in both eyes by five.
The school's books used large raised letters that students traced slowly, and students could not write with them.

Charles Barbier, a retired artillery captain, made night writing: a code of twelve raised dots representing sounds so soldiers could communicate in the dark; soldiers found it too hard and it was never accepted.
Barbier presented his invention to the school for the blind; twelve-year-old Louis spent the next two years improving it.
Barbier's 2 x 6 grid was too tall to read in a single go with one finger.
Braille reduced it to six dots, three high and two wide, representing letters rather than sounds, small enough to fit in a fingertip.
Braille's cells could be recognized as letters with a single touch of a finger, and he built the system using Barbier's slate and stylus.
Teachers refused to recognize the code; Braille died at 43 in 1852; the Institute adopted it in 1854 because of the blind pupils' insistence.
Braille brought education to millions across the globe.

cast.louis: a 12 year old thin French boy with straight short black hair and a fringe, a pale narrow face, eyes half closed and unfocused, a navy blue wool school jacket with a high collar over a white shirt, 1820s
cast.child: a 4 year old small boy with blond curly hair, chubby pink cheeks and a loose white linen smock, 1810s
cast.barbier: a 54 year old tall lean retired French artillery captain with swept-back silver hair, long grey sideburns, a hawk nose and a faded dark blue military coat with red cuffs and brass buttons, 1820s
cast.teacher: a 40 year old thin stern French teacher with dark hair slicked flat, a pointed black chin beard and a black frock coat with a tall white collar, 1840s
